activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
story:
The note was folded into a square and tucked inside Gavin's lunch bag, in Viviane's round handwriting: "Burned the toast AGAIN this morning. My brother says it's just melted, like ice. Physical change. Is he right? Bring evidence. Viviane." Gavin read it twice, then looked down at his own sandwich and grinned. Today Ms. Clarke-Williams had promised them the lab with the hot plates, and this was his chance to settle it.

"Toast," he announced, dropping his bag on the counter beside Viviane and Betty. "We're testing toast." Betty raised an eyebrow, but she helped him set out two slices of bread, a plate of ice cubes, and a magnifying lens while the hot plate ticked and warmed. The lab smelled like vinegar from the period before, sharp enough to make Gavin's nose wrinkle. He laid an ice cube on a tray and watched it pool into clear water. "Physical change," he said. "It can go back to ice in the freezer."

"But toast can't go back," Viviane said slowly, watching the bread on the hot plate. The edges had turned pale gold, then deeper brown, and a smell like Sunday morning drifted up, warm and almost sweet. Gavin bent close with the lens. The surface wasn't just darker. It was different, rough and blistered where it had been smooth.

"That's it," he said. "I can deduce it from the color. Melting doesn't make new colors, it just changes shape. But this brown stuff is new. It didn't exist in the soft bread." He flipped the toast with tongs, and the underside had gone nearly black at one corner where he'd left it too long against the rim. Betty poked the burnt edge with a pencil. It crumbled.

"So could my brother fix it?" Viviane asked. "If he's right, he just melts it back."

Gavin shook his head. "He can't. It's a chemical change, because heat creates new brown substances and the toast cannot turn back into soft bread. That's the difference. Ice goes back. Toast never does." Viviane wrote it down word for word on the back of her note, as if it were a message from the frontier of science, some place no one had mapped yet.

Ms. Clarke-Williams drifted past their station and sniffed the air. "Bread, Gavin? Interesting choice." He held up the burnt slice and the melted ice cube side by side. "One goes back," he said, "and one never does." She smiled and moved on, and Betty leaned over the counter.

"Text your brother," she told Viviane. "Tell him toast beats ice."

Viviane pulled out her phone, thumbs already flying, and Gavin slid the perfect golden slice onto a napkin and broke it in half, offering the bigger piece to Betty.

story:
Easton tugged the lion head over his shoulders and blinked through the mesh eyes. The gymnasium behind the community temple smelled like incense from the hall next door, and the drums were already thumping in his chest. In two weeks, the temple's New Year gathering would feature the lion dance, and Ms. Leung had chosen him and Hope to perform it. He could not wait.

"Lion dance has two dancers," Hope said from behind him, her hands on his waist. "One in the head, one in the tail. Same costume." That was the rule, and it was the problem too, because every time Easton stepped left, Hope stepped right, and the whole lion collapsed in a tangle of red and gold fur.

They tripped again. Easton sat on the floor, breathing hard, and remembered the video he had watched three nights ago, when the idea first sparked. The lion in that video had moved like a single animal, front legs and back legs flowing together, and at the time he had assumed the dancers were just lucky. Now he suspected something hidden: the two dancers could not see each other at all, so they had to be following the same signal. The drums, the gongs, the cymbals. The music was telling both of them when to move.

"Test it," he said, jumping up. "Don't watch me. Listen. One drumbeat, I step forward. You step forward too. Gong means jump."

They tried it. Drum, drum, both feet landed together. Gong, and the lion leapt, fur rippling, tail snapping behind. It worked so well that Charlize, who had been categorizing the costumes into repair piles by the wall, dropped her clipboard and cheered. "You look like one creature!" she shouted. "Like a real lion!"

Ms. Leung watched from the doorway, then changed her mind about the schedule. "You're ready to perform at the gathering," she announced. "Not just the practice demonstration. The real one."

Later, drying sweat from his neck, Easton overheard a grandparent telling Charlize that many dancers in the temple troupe were descendants of the original founders, and that this gathering was considered the most prestigious one in the neighborhood. Easton grinned so wide his cheeks hurt.

When the drums started again, he lifted the head, felt Hope's hands settle on his waist, and together they sprang forward into the golden light.

story:
At the reunion, the whole back garden smelled of sausages and cut grass, and Zachary stood with his cousins in a line, feet wide, waiting. In two weeks his school group would perform the haka Ka Mate to welcome new families at the community hall, and Uncle Hone had promised to check his form today. Zachary stamped, slapped his thighs, and puffed out his chest, but his feet kept tangling on the third move. The practice video was ambiguous about which foot went first there, and he had assumed it was the left, because most of the dance favoured the left. He had been wrong before with assumptions. Last year he had quit the school kapa haka group after one rehearsal because he felt clumsy, and he still wasn't sure whether that had been sensible or just lazy.

"Hold," said Uncle Hone, tapping his own knee. "Again, from the top. Slow."

Zachary went again, slower. He had a new idea: instead of copying the whole sequence at once, he would break the moves apart the way Ms. Kamau, his science teacher, described a decomposer breaking a fallen log into pieces an ecosystem can use. Third move only, ten times. Then the third and fourth together. It was tedious, but by the seventh repetition his feet stopped arguing with him, and by the tenth the pattern felt like walking.

"Why do we shout the words so loud?" his cousin Alaric asked, wiping his forehead.

"Because of what they're about," Uncle Hone said. "Ka Mate was composed around 1820 by the Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha. He'd been hiding from enemies who were chasing him, and when he came out alive, he made this to celebrate surviving."

So the stomping was not just noise, Zachary thought; it was a man's heartbeat after coming out of hiding. He stamped the third move, hard, both feet planted.

"That one," he said. "Watch this."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
story:
Emilie had exactly one hour before her class project was due, and the account with all her slides was locked. She had used her old password, the one from the game site, and it no longer worked because last spring she had let her cousin guess it in about four seconds. She still remembered her cousin's grin, and she still felt annoyed at herself for choosing her cat's name followed by the number one.

The repair shop worker at the computer store near her house leaned over the counter and clicked through the account page. "You can't get your old password back, because the site doesn't have it," he said. "Well-run websites store a hash of each password, a scrambled one-way fingerprint, instead of the password itself." He drew a quick squiggle on a napkin to show how the letters of her password might look after the site scrambled them. "They can check a login without keeping the real password. That's why they can only let you make a new one, never tell you the old one."

Emilie stared at the squiggle. So the site held a fingerprint, not the password itself. That meant nobody at the site could read her password even if they wanted to, which felt strange but also somehow safe, like a translucent window that let light through without showing her face. She thought about the game site where she had reused that same password everywhere. If one site leaked its fingerprints, someone could try her password on other sites too. That was the pattern she had never seen before, and now she couldn't stop seeing it.

She typed a new password, something long and odd, and wrote a hint on a card she kept in her desk drawer at home, under a small hierarchy of papers organized by subject, homework on top. Then she opened her slides and submitted the project with six minutes to spare. Her friend Maeve texted, "Did you make it?" Emilie sent back the napkin squiggle, photographed on the counter. "New password. It's called a hash, sort of. Long story. Ask me at school."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
story:
Brayden sat on the spinning stool at ClearVision Optical, twenty minutes before his mom's car had to be back at the garage. The optometrist had already told him his vision was 20/200, which meant the big E at the top of the chart had been a blurry smudge. Now he had to pick frames before the store closed at five, and the clock above the register read 4:41.

He tried on a pair of black wire frames and looked in the mirror. Behind him, Alessio and Felicia sat on the bench by the window, passing a bag of pretzels back and forth.

"You look like Mr. Katz," Alessio said.

"I do not." Brayden squinted at his reflection. He kind of did.

Felicia held up her phone. "My cousin in Australia just texted me. She says she has six-six vision and she's really proud of it. Is that better than Brayden's twenty-something?"

Alessio shrugged. "Six is smaller than twenty, so probably worse?"

Brayden took the phone and read the message himself. His cousin was bragging, the way you brag about good eyes. He thought about the eye chart on the wall, the letters he'd squinted at all morning. The numbers on charts measured the same thing. Six-six had to be their way of writing perfect vision, the same as twenty-twenty, because countries that used metres would measure distance differently. It was like spelling "color" as "colour."

"I think six-six is the same as twenty-twenty," he said. "Australia uses metres, so they write it different. Her eyes are just normal."

The optometrist, passing by with a tray of lenses, nodded. "That's right."

"See, she's not better than anyone," Brayden said, handing the phone back. Some small resentment about the bragging faded, which surprised him.

The wire frames pinched his nose. He swapped them for round tortoiseshell ones and the world in the mirror still looked soft, because the lenses were plain glass until his real prescription arrived. Through the window he could see the lush green of the hedge along the parking lot, one blurry green mass.

"They'll preserve your new lenses if you get the coating," the clerk said. "Scratch guard."

"Get it," Brayden said. His mom was already at the counter, pulling out her card.

He put the glasses back on and looked at the wall of frames, each one suddenly sharp-edged and separate, all the little screws visible. "Whoa," he said. "Those have screws?"

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
story:
Kaylee sat in the dentist's waiting room, kicking her sneakers against the chair leg and reading the same poster about flossing for the fourth time. Across the room, her classmate Cale was hunched over, gripping the armrests of his chair like it might bolt for the door. He wasn't even here for an appointment; he'd come along with his older sister. "You okay?" Kaylee asked. Cale shook his head. "My chest feels tight and my heart's going crazy. I think something's really wrong with me." His breathing went fast and shallow, and the paper cup of water in his hand crumpled until the water dwindled down to a few drops on the carpet.

Kaylee's first reasoning went like this: tight chest plus racing heart equals call somebody, immediately. She shot up and waved down Ms. Anderson, the dental hygienist, who crouched beside Cale and felt his pulse. While she checked him, something odd happened. Cale's breathing slowed on its own, and the color came back into his face, and after a few minutes he said the squeezing feeling was almost gone. "That was so weird," he mumbled. "It hit me out of nowhere and it was like the worst it could possibly get, and now it's just... leaving."

"It sounds like a panic attack," Ms. Anderson said quietly. "It's a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes. It can feel like a heart attack even though it isn't one." Kaylee blinked. That was exactly backwards from what she'd assumed, that scary things only get worse until a doctor fixes them. She'd been ready to sprint down the hall screaming for an ambulance, and instead the peak had come and gone like a wave hitting the beach.

"Subjective," Kaylee said slowly, trying out a word from her vocabulary homework. "It felt like a heart attack, but the feeling wasn't the facts." Cale managed a weak grin. "Thanks, walking dictionary." Ms. Anderson said Cale's sister and his parents should hear about it from him today, so a grown-up who knew him could keep an eye out, and Cale nodded and pulled out his phone. Kaylee slid the crumpled cup into the trash and dropped into the chair beside him. "Next time your chest does that," she said, "squeeze my hand instead of the cup. The cups are innocent."

Mathis had to sit with his knees pulled up because his sneakers pressed against the heater vent, and even that didn't help. "Dad, my shoes feel like clown shoes are coming. I mean they don't fit. Again."

"Again?" His dad glanced over from the driver's seat. "We bought those in September."

"That's the bizarre part," Mathis said, wiggling his toes against the toe of the shoe. "September. And look at my jeans." He smoothed his hands down his legs. "Still fine. Not even short."

They pulled into the mall parking lot, and Mathis was already unbuckling. At the shoe store, the cashier measured his foot and raised her eyebrows. "Size up a full size and a half since fall," she said. "That's a big jump."

Mathis stared at the metal measuring thing like it was treasure. A full size and a half, while his jeans still fit. He turned the fact over the whole time his dad paid. His feet were somehow ahead of the rest of him, running a race his legs hadn't started yet. He had assumed growing up would happen all at once, like a plant shooting up evenly, but the evidence said otherwise. Feet first, apparently, then everything else.

He tested his idea on the way to the food court. "Dad, hold on. If feet grow before legs do, then I bet my arms are going to be next. Or my legs. Something's coming." He held up his hands and studied them. "These are, like, the candidates. The scouts. The advance team."

His dad laughed so hard he had to set down the tray. "The advance team. I'd like a report when they arrive."

Monday morning, Mathis found Adelina at her locker before the bell. "Adelina. Scientific question. If your feet get bigger and your jeans still fit, what does that mean?" She squinted at him. "It means you're about to get tall," he said, grinning. "I'm expecting a growth spurt any day now. I'll keep records. Shoe box receipts and everything." He looked down at his brand-new sneakers, still blindingly white, and pointed his toes down the hall.

story:
Anna wanted a new profile picture before Monday, and the mall fountain made a good backdrop, with its polished stone and the big skylight overhead. Malory leaned in on one side and McKayla on the other, and a passing stranger offered to take the shot so all three could be in it. He took two photos on Anna's phone and walked off toward the food court.

"Post the second one," McKayla said. "My hair wasn't ready in the first." Anna sat on the fountain's edge to look through them. She zoomed in on McKayla's hoodie, where the letters of their school, Jefferson Middle, sat right above the crest. Then she zoomed further, past Malory's shoulder, to the mall directory mounted on the pillar behind them. The strip of shops along the bottom was labelled Millbrook Road. She scrolled back out and looked at the whole picture again. Somebody who had never met them could read a school name and a street name off one photo, and the mall had exactly one entrance on Millbrook Road.

She tried an experiment. She asked Malory and McKayla to slide down the bench until the directory was out of the frame, then she swapped positions so the school crest faced away from the camera. "Can you demonstrate the new pose one more time?" she asked, and McKayla flipped her hood inside out and grinned. Anna took the photo herself, zoomed in, and checked every corner. Wall, plants, skylight. Nothing that named a street, a school, or a house number anywhere.

"Since when do you care?" Malory asked.

"Since a guy I've never met just held my phone," Anna said. She posted the clean picture and put her phone in her pocket.

At the science store window, an ear model made of rubbery cartilage stood beside a jar marked with a toxic symbol from some chemistry kit. "We should get that for Ms. Lavoie's room," McKayla said, tapping the glass. Anna pulled her phone back out, framed the two of them with the ear behind them, and said, "Okay, but check the background first."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
story:
The word card said "colour," and Florence felt her stomach drop. She was standing at the front of Mr. Chowdhury's classroom, the last three spellers left in the school bee, and the judges had just handed her a word she had argued about only two weeks ago.

"Can I have the language of origin?" she asked.

"English," said Mr. Chowdhury, who was reading from the official list.

Florence's mind went back to the lunch table, where Liam had been waving his phone around. His cousin in Toronto had sent him a photo of her school spelling list, and half the words looked wrong to him. "Colour," he had said. "Honour. They spell it with a u up there. Who's right?"

They had looked it up together in the library instead of going outside. Florence had found the answer in a dusty reference book while Liam leaned over her shoulder so close she had to compress herself into the corner of the chair to keep reading. Before 1828, English spellings were a tangle, and then Noah Webster's American Dictionary of the English Language pushed simpler spellings, like "color" instead of "colour," and those became standard in the United States. Neither spelling was really wrong. They just belonged to different places, like two doors out of the same room.

Katia, sitting in the second row now, mouthed something at her. Florence couldn't read it. The clock on the wall hung slightly off true, tilted a few degrees from perpendicular, and she fixed her eyes on it to steady herself.

Here was the trap. At lunch, Liam had said the school bee would follow American convention, but Florence had never actually checked the rules sheet. She thought about it now, fast. This was a school bee in Ohio. The pronouncer had given every other word in American spelling when he read the vocabulary sentences. If the card said "colour," then the judges wanted the British spelling, and they had written it that way on purpose to see if spellers knew it was a variant, not a mistake. If she spelled it the American way, she might be marked wrong.

"C-o-l-o-u-r," she said. "Colour."

Mr. Chowdhury checked his sheet and nodded. "That is correct."

Liam, eliminated three rounds earlier on "manoeuvre," smacked the desk softly. "You remembered the lunch argument."

After the bee, which Florence won on the word "perpendicular" of all things, she found Liam by the door. He was holding his phone, probably about to text his cousin the news.

"So who won the spelling war?" he asked. "Webster or the Canadians?"

Florence thought about the book in the library, about her own choice to look things up instead of guessing. "Nobody," she said. "They just went through different doors." She tucked her trophy under her arm and pushed open the classroom door.

story:
Ryan sat on the end of his bed with a printed page in his hands, one he had grabbed off Ms. Bighorn's classroom shelf before the bell rang. His left knuckle still stung where he had punched his desk that afternoon, after Rudy had grabbed his sketchbook and held it open above his head for the whole bus line to see. Ryan hadn't planned to hit anything. His hand had simply gone before the rest of him could vote.

The page was from a science magazine. He read the same sentence three times: the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. He put the page down on his quilt and looked at his hand, then at the wall above his desk, where a dent from a thrown controller still marked the paint from last spring.

He flashed back to that afternoon, seconds before the desk punch. Rudy waving the sketchbook, the crowd laughing, Isra saying "just give it back," and then a kind of white gap where the punch should have been in his memory. It was like trying to remember a hallway with the lights off. He had walked through it, but he couldn't see it.

That was the part that interested him. If the planning part of his brain was still under construction, then maybe the gap wasn't him being a bad person. Maybe it was like trying to drive a car that was still getting its brakes installed. He decided to test it. He took out a notebook and wrote a rule at the top: any time Rudy grabs something, count to five before moving. It was a way of lending the unfinished part of his brain a substitute. He couldn't eliminate the impulse, but he could build a wall around the part where his hand decided things on its own.

At school the next morning, Rudy snatched the notebook itself right off Ryan's desk. Ryan felt the same hot spark go off behind his eyes, and he counted. One, two, three. Isra leaned over from the next seat and said, "That's the prefrontal cortex thing you were reading about, right? The part that plans stuff?" Ryan nodded, still counting. Five. Then he stood up, walked to Ms. Bighorn's desk, and said, "Rudy has my notebook and I'd like it back." Rudy blinked, handed it over without a joke, and the class went back to its worksheet.

At lunch Ryan told them the whole story, including the dent in his wall, as an anecdote about the controller. "It sounded smart at the time," he admitted. "Thinking I'd never get frustrated." "That was a little naive," Isra said, and Rudy laughed so hard milk came out his nose. Ryan laughed too, and slid the notebook, safely, into the bottom of his backpack.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
story:
Sarah stood on a kitchen chair in the living room because it felt more like a podium, and held her note cards at an angle nearly perpendicular to the floor, which made them impossible to read. "Two minutes," her mother said from the couch, thumb on the timer. "Opening hook, three points, closing. Go." Sarah opened with a question about school lunches, listed her three points about longer recess, and then mumbled toward the end, "So, yeah. Thanks for listening." The timer read one minute forty. "Your closing just kind of fell off a cliff," her mother said gently. "Want to try Devon's trick? He practiced in front of his dog."

That was the problem. Sarah had a strong hook and three solid points, but the ending slid away from her like the last bit of a smoothie through a straw. She flopped onto the rug and stared at the ceiling, where a water stain looked like a lopsided map. Then she remembered Ms. Côté's class, the day they had listened to a recording of a speech from 1963. Martin Luther King Jr. had said "I have a dream" over and over, and even kids who doodled through everything had sat still for it. When Devon asked afterward why it worked, Ms. Côté had said only, "Repeating the same words at the start of several sentences is called anaphora," and refused to say more, which drove everyone crazy. Sarah sat up so fast her pulse seemed to accelerate.

Maybe the repetition itself was the principle, the thing doing the work, like a drumbeat you could feel in the floor. She grabbed a fresh card and wrote four sentences, each one starting the same way: "Recess gives us time to think. Recess gives us time to move. Recess gives us a reason to love Tuesday afternoons. Recess gives us back our brains." She read them aloud to the ceiling and grinned, because the fourth one made her laugh every time.

She climbed back onto the chair and tapped her cards straight. "Timer," she said. Her mother smiled and held up her thumb. "Two minutes. Go."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
story:
The after-school culture club was making a display for the hallway bulletin board, and Kaitlyn wanted her section to be the best one. Every member had drawn a small map with arrows showing where their families had come from. Imane had drawn Morocco and Canada with a bold line between them, and Charly had taped a photo of a grandmother's kitchen in Manila. Kaitlyn's own arrows were easy, from Ireland and from Mexico to here, but the new boy, whose name tag still said hello, I'm Adnan, had drawn nothing at all.

"Where are you from?" she asked him, because that was the whole point of the map.

Adnan turned his pencil over and over in his fingers. "I've lived in Turkey, then Malaysia, then Egypt, and now here," he said. "My parents are from Pakistan. But I was born in Turkey, so I don't really." He stopped and started again. "Every time someone asks, I feel like my answer is too long, and it must sound made up."

Kaitlyn frowned. Everyone else at the table had answered in one word, and his answer needed four countries plus one more. She wondered whether there was a word for a person whose answer was a whole list. While the others worked, she went to the library cart that Mr. Ngo had wheeled in beside the art supplies, the one stacked with books about families and migration. She flipped through one about children who move around the world, and there it was in the second chapter. An American sociologist named Ruth Hill Useem had coined the term "third culture kid" back in the 1950s, for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. Kaitlyn read the sentence three times to be sure she had it right.

She carried the book back to the table and set it down in front of Adnan. "Third culture kid," she said. "That's an actual term. A sociologist made it up."

Adnan looked at the page, then at her. "That's a legitimate thing? People study it?"

"Look at the author and the date," Kaitlyn said, pointing. "It's real."

Charly leaned over. "So Adnan's map needs five arrows."

"No," said Adnan, and for the first time that afternoon he smiled. "It needs a circle. All the places, and me in the middle." He began to draw, and Imane offered him her good colored pencils, which she never lent to anyone, a small ritual she performed only when something mattered.

Kaitlyn went back to her own arrows and found that they didn't diminish next to his circle. They were just different, side by side on the same board. When Mr. Ngo came by to check the display, he studied Adnan's circle for a long moment, then gave a slow nod and wrote something in his notebook.

At the end of the meeting, Adnan tore a corner off his scrap paper and copied the title of the book. "For my little sister," he said. "She hates that question too."

"Tell her there's a name for it," Kaitlyn said, and slid the colored pencils back across the table to Imane.

story:
Paisley sat in the computer lab during lunch, refreshing the school club page for the third time. The Robotics Club roster was gone, replaced by a plain notice: "Page under repair." She needed the list because she had promised Mr. Demir she would delegate jobs to each member before Friday's build session, and now she couldn't remember who had signed up for the sensor team.

Iris leaned over from the next computer. "It was up yesterday. I read the whole thing, even the part where Yuna wrote her name in all capitals. YUNA. Like she was announcing an emperor."

Paisley laughed, then stopped. Yesterday. Something nagged at her, and it wasn't the roster. Yesterday she had also seen a different page, the one from last month, the one where the club's old president had posted a photo of Paisley mid-sneeze with the caption "Club mascot." She had been so relieved when someone told her the post was deleted. She had even gone back to check, twice, and it was gone. Deleted meant gone, she had decided. Like erasing a whiteboard.

"Can I borrow your screen?" Paisley asked. Iris slid over. Paisley typed the way Mr. Demir had shown the class one afternoon, on a site he called the Wayback Machine. She remembered him saying only one sentence about it, that it had saved more than one trillion web pages. A trillion. She had thought that sounded like a made-up number, like something a kid would invent to win an argument.

She typed the club page's address and clicked the snapshot dated last month. The page rebuilt itself, sneeze photo and all. Paisley stared at her own crumpled face, mouth open, one hand mid-air.

"Whoa," Iris said. "I thought it was deleted."

"It was." Paisley pointed at the address bar. "It's saved here anyway. Deleted from the page, not from everywhere."

"So the roster might be too," Iris said. "From before the repair."

Paisley typed again, found a snapshot from Tuesday, and there it was: seventeen names, sensor team circled in green marker by whoever had scanned the sign-up sheet. She copied the names onto her palm with a pen.

Yuna appeared in the doorway, lunch bag swinging. "You found it? Wait. Is that the sneeze picture?"

Paisley closed the old snapshot slowly, the way you close a door you don't want to hear. "It was only ever supposed to be temporary," she said.

"Two dots," Liv said. "That's it? That's your room?"

"They're vanishing points." Alexis set a fresh hard pencil against the paper. "Every edge of the room has to point at one of them. Watch, I'll draft the walls first, all light, like scaffolding." She drew a vertical line for the corner of the far wall, then angled lines out from its top and bottom toward each dot. Soon the page held a whole network of faint lines, fanning out in every direction, with a box of a room caught in the middle of it. "Can I try?" Liv grabbed a soft pencil, the dark one, and pressed hard as she drew a line from the corner toward the left dot. The line gouged shiny gray into the paper. Alexis drew the window, darkened the real edges of the room, then reached for her eraser and swept it across the network of guide lines.

Half of them came away. Liv's line did not.

Alexis erased again, harder. The line only turned smudgy, a ghost stamped into the paper. She rubbed until the eraser squeaked, and the line sat there, bold as a fence post, cutting straight through her window.

"Liv. Look." Alexis held the sketchbook up to the light, and the groove Liv had pressed shone back at them. "You carved it in. It won't come out."

Liv winced. "My brother says our stubbornness is hereditary. Maybe my pencil has it too."

From the other side of the fence, Ms. Smith leaned over, watering can still in hand. "What's the disaster over there?"

"Nothing," Alexis called back, though she was already testing an idea. She took the hard pencil and drew one more guide line, barely touching the paper, quick as a whisper. She darkened a shelf edge over it, then erased. The guide line vanished clean, leaving only the shelf. So that was the trick. Light hands for the guides, heavy hands for the real edges, and the room stayed a room.

"New page," she said, and turned it herself. "This time you get the hard pencil. One line, feather light. If you can see yourself pressing, you're pressing."

Liv took the hard pencil and hovered over the paper like it might bite. "Feather light," she repeated, and drew a line so faint they had to tilt the page to find it.

"Perfect," Alexis said, and pinned the corner of the sketchbook down before the breeze could argue.

story:
Hailey squeezed onto the couch between Damon and Conner, balancing her plate of nachos on her knees while Ms. Morningstar turned up the volume on the big game. The whole living room smelled like popcorn, and through the window the neighbor's lush green hedge swayed in the wind. With two minutes left in the fourth quarter, the score was tied, and everybody in the room was yelling at the same television.

During a timeout, Conner frowned at the screen. "Why do they even call it a basket? The thing's a metal hoop with a net. There's no basket anywhere."

"A net's kind of like a basket," Damon said, shrugging.

Hailey chewed her nacho slowly while she thought. Names usually came from somewhere, and she liked figuring out where. If the game was called basketball, maybe once the goals really had been baskets. She remembered the old peach basket she'd seen hanging on the wall of Ms. Morningstar's garage when they were getting the folding chairs, painted white and cracked at the rim. That could be a clue. "I'll be right back," she said, and slipped out to the garage before Conner could ask why.

She found the basket exactly where she remembered it, beside the rake and a box of garden tools. When she carried it back into the living room, the timeout was still running, and Ms. Morningstar smiled at it like an old friend.

"That belonged to my grandfather," Ms. Morningstar said. "He taught gym for forty years and told this story every single December."

Hailey held up the basket. "So this is why it's called basketball? Real baskets?"

"That's the story he told," Ms. Morningstar said. "James Naismith invented the game in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he used peach baskets as the goals."

"A peach basket," Conner repeated, staring at it. "So somebody threw a ball into a peach basket and invented a whole sport."

Hailey tried to assess whether that could really be true, turning the basket over in her hands the way a scientist might. It was deep, which meant the ball would get stuck after every score. Somebody would have to climb up and fish it out every time. "It's kind of a terrible goal," she said. "But it must have worked, because here we all are." Damon laughed so hard a chip fell off his plate.

The buzzer sounded and the game came back on, but Hailey kept thinking about a cold gym in Massachusetts more than a hundred years ago, a teacher nailing a basket to a wall. Conner leaned over and whispered, "You solve mysteries now?" She set the peach basket on the coffee table, right where everyone could see it, and pointed at the screen as the point guard drove toward the hoop.

"Watch," she said. "This one's going in."

Olivier's bike chain had slipped three times on the ride home, and now the bike hung upside down from two ropes in Mr. Shin's garage workshop, spinning slowly while Olivier stared at it. Khalid sat on an upturned crate, eating crackers he had brought for no reason anyone could name.

"Rust," Khalid said, crumbs falling. "Every chain that slips is rusted. My cousin's bike, my brother's bike, the one at school. All rusted."

"So the chain is the problem because it's rusted," Olivier said slowly. "That's my hypothesis. A guess I can test." He wiped the chain with a rag until it gleamed. The links moved smoothly, no orange anywhere, not even in the corners. Then he turned the pedal with his hand, and the chain slipped off the rear sprocket anyway, dropping onto the garage floor with a clank that made Mr. Shin look over from the workbench where he was repairing a lamp for his neighbor.

"Not rust," Olivier said. He picked up the chain and laid it along the sprocket, matching link to tooth. Halfway around, the links rode up on the teeth instead of seating into them. He got the ruler from Mr. Shin's drawer and measured the teeth at four points around the wheel. Three measurements matched. The fourth was almost two millimeters shorter. The wear wasn't symmetrical; one section of the sprocket had been ground down, probably from a year of pedaling hard on the same stretch of road where the hill started.

"Here's the thing," Olivier said, holding up the chain. "I could wipe down a hundred clean chains and it wouldn't prove your rust idea, because finding more rusty ones doesn't settle it. But this one chain, clean as a spoon, slips anyway. That kills it. Like swans, Mr. Shin says. You can't prove all swans are white by counting white swans, but one black swan proves the claim false." Khalid frowned at his crackers for a while, then shrugged and handed one to Olivier, which was their usual compromise.

Mr. Shin found a replacement sprocket in a box marked FREE, TAKE, DON'T ASK, and said Olivier could have it for the price of sweeping the floor. "Better than my pension pays," he added, and turned back to his lamp. Olivier unbolted the old sprocket, pressed the new one on, threaded the chain, and flipped the bike upright. He spun the pedals. The chain ran around and around, quiet and even, and did not come off once.

Emile was eating toast at the kitchen table with his tablet propped against the nectar bottle, because that was the only spot the hummingbird feeder juice hadn't dripped on, when his class chat lit up. He typed a joke about the math homework: "Ms. Ndlovu said we can skip the whole assignment if we bring her a coffee." It was obviously ridiculous. He hit send and went back to his toast.

Two minutes later Paula messaged him privately. "Are you serious? Is that allowed? I don't have a coffee. Should I bring money instead?" Then Nixon posted in the group: "PAULA IS WALKING TO THE CAFE RIGHT NOW." Emile groaned. At school, if he'd said it out loud, Paula would have heard his voice going silly on the word "coffee" and laughed. In here his words just sat there, flat, with nothing wrapped around them. He typed "IT WAS A JOGG" and deleted it, because spelling errors would only irritate her more when she was already halfway to the cafe.

He set down his toast and wondered. Somebody must have noticed this problem before, right? People writing to each other without faces, jokes landing like bricks. He searched "how to show a message is a joke." That led him to a page about a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman, who had proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Emile stared at the little sideways face. Nearly forty years before Emile was typing, a grown man had solved Emile's exact problem with three marks on a keyboard. He copied it and pasted it after his joke in the group chat: "Bring her a coffee :-)"

Paula wrote back within seconds. "Oh. OH. Why didn't you put the face on it the first time?" Nixon sent a row of laughing faces, which felt like showing off, like his whole personality was somehow more sophisticated than Emile's three humble marks. Emile tried it on his little brother at dinner, saying "the dog ate my homework" with a straight face, and got no reaction until he drew :-) on a napkin and slid it across the table.

The next morning Ms. Ndlovu collected the assignments and looked at Emile over her glasses. "I hear there was a coffee involved." "It was a joke," Emile said. "I had to prove it." She held out her hand, palm up, waiting, so he drew the smiley in the air with his finger and she nodded once and moved on down the row.

Theo pressed the measuring cup into the bag of flour and packed it full, then leveled it off with the back of a knife, the way he always did. Ms. Warsame's community kitchen smelled like butter and cinnamon, and tonight he was making cookies for his family's Friday dinner, the batch he'd been promising for two weeks. His little sister had asked for soft, bendy cookies, the kind you could fold without breaking, and he intended to deliver.

He had made this recipe once before, at home, and the cookies had come out dry and cakey, more like muffin tops than cookies. He'd followed every step meticulously, so it made no sense. He'd blamed the oven, then the butter, and finally given up.

Hashim leaned over the counter beside him, stirring his own bowl of granola. "Mine always work," Hashim said, a little too cheerfully. He wanted to win the kitchen's mini baking table this month, and the chocolate chip category was still open. "Maybe you just have bad cookie karma."

"Karma isn't real," Theo said. "Something else is going on." He looked at his cup of flour, then at the recipe card. It said two and a quarter cups. He had measured exactly that at home too. So what was different?

Vera shrugged. "My grandma showed me. Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects. Weighing flour is more accurate." She tapped the scale. "I aim for the same grams every time now."

Theo stood still, holding his packed cup. If his cup held too much flour, then his dough had too much flour in it, even though he'd measured right. That could be why it came out dry and cakey. It was like steering a boat with a bent rudder: he'd been aiming correctly the whole time, but something underneath pushed him off course.

He asked Vera if he could borrow the scale, and she slid it over. He tapped his packed cup of flour out into a bowl on the scale and read the number. Then he spooned flour gently into another cup, leveled it, and weighed that. The numbers were different. He weighed out what the recipe card listed in grams, one bowl at a time, and mixed his dough. It looked softer and glossier than his batch at home, and it sagged a little when he dropped spoonfuls onto the pan.

While the cookies baked, Hashim sneaked over and weighed a scoop of his own flour. He wrote the number on his wrist with a pen, frowning. "I've been packing mine too," he admitted. "Every single batch." The timer rang, and Theo pulled the pan out. The cookies were golden at the edges and soft in the middle, and he bent one gently in half. It folded without breaking. Vera looked over and said, "That one's going on the table board."

"Two to three times as deep as the seed is wide," Sarah read off the back of the bean packet, frowning at it like it had insulted her.

The problem was simple: the block party was on Saturday, and Ms. Mendoza had promised a prize for the best backyard garden, which was a problem because Sarah's backyard was currently a rectangle of dirt with three seed packets sitting on it. Worse, it might rain that very night, and rain would turn her careful plans into mud. She and Cecelia knelt in the grass beside the patch, sorting seeds on a paper towel. Cecelia held up a bean seed and then a carrot seed, and the two of them looked so ridiculous side by side that Sarah laughed. The bean was fat as a fingernail. The carrot seed was smaller than a freckle.

"Last year I dug every hole the same," Sarah said, poking a trowel into the soil. She flashed back to the summer before, standing over this same patch with her dad, dropping beans into holes deep enough to hide a marble, then sprinkling carrot seeds on top like confetti. Nothing had come up. Not one green hook, not one leaf. She had blamed the birds, then the fungus she'd read about, then the universe. Now, staring at the two seeds, a suspicion tickled her. A bean could push up through a lot of dirt. A freckle-sized seed probably couldn't push through any. The packet line suddenly wasn't gibberish. It was arithmetic.

So they tested it. For the beans, Sarah measured with her finger: one knuckle deep, a bit more, roughly three bean-widths down. For the carrots, Cecelia barely scratched the surface and pressed the tiny seeds in with one fingertip, which was so tedious that Cecelia narrated it in a news-anchor voice: "The nation waits. The carrot enters the soil. Depth: practically nothing." They covered everything, then spread straw over the bed to insulate the soil against the cold night coming. Alex arrived halfway through with a watering can and an announcement that he had brought "moral support and also a juice box." Sarah made him measure the pea holes himself. He got it wrong twice before he caught on, and Cecelia awarded him the juice box as a trophy.

By the time the sky went pewter-colored, the rain was tapping the fence. They dashed inside with dirt to their elbows. On Saturday morning Sarah ran out barefoot and stopped dead at the fence. A curved green hook stood where the beans went in, and along the carrot row the soil had cracked in a dozen tiny places, like something small was knocking. Alex leaned over the fence and said, "The freckles are winning."

Camille spread her parts across the picnic table at the edge of the skate park: one battery, one bulb, one switch, three wires. Behind her, wheels rattled down the concrete bowls, but she kept her eyes on the little pile. Cecily dropped onto the bench beside her, still holding her board. "Did you fix the box lamp?" she asked. The old lamp on the storage box had been dead for months, and Cecily wanted light so the older kids could keep skating after sunset. "I'm getting there," Camille said. "Ms. Becker saw me carrying the battery this morning and said I could try, but only if I did it right."

She connected the first wire from the battery to the switch, then the second from the switch to the bulb. The last wire would close the loop back to the battery. Her fingers felt clumsy and rebellious, and the wire kept slipping off the screw, but she tightened it a little at a time until it held. Before she attached the final wire, Nayla leaned over the table. "Just stick that one straight across the battery ends," Nayla said, grabbing a bare wire. "Shortcut it."

Camille caught her wrist. At the hardware store two days ago, she had heard Ms. Becker stop another kid who was about to do exactly that. "Don't join the battery's two ends with nothing in between," Ms. Becker had said then. "That's a short circuit, and it lets a large current flow that can make the wire and the battery dangerously hot." Now Camille repeated the words. "A short circuit. The wire would get hot enough to burn you." Nayla set the wire down slowly, like it had turned into something with teeth.

Instead, Camille clipped the last wire from the bulb back to the battery's free end and pressed the switch. The bulb lit, but its glow began to fluctuate, brightening and dimming over and over. "It did that before," Cecily said, which Camille took as useful testimony, since Cecily had watched her earlier failed attempts. Camille studied the setup. The pattern had to mean the current was stopping and starting somewhere she couldn't see. She pushed firmly on the switch's metal tab while the bulb glowed, and the flickering stopped. The contact underneath was loose. She pried the tab up a hair with her thumbnail so it pressed tighter, and the light steadied into a clean, even shine.

That evening, after the lamp on the storage box blazed and the first board rolled past in its glow, Camille found a folded note taped to her front door. "It's still on," Cecily had written. "I skated till eight. Bring the battery tomorrow. Nayla wants to try the buzzer." Camille tucked the note in her pocket and went inside to pack her wires.

Grandma's kitchen smelled like cinnamon, and the old thermostat by the door read seventy-two even though it felt colder, which was typical of Grandpa's house. Anna spread her Spanish homework across the table. She was supposed to describe her family in full sentences, and she had until Sunday to record herself saying them out loud without reading.

"Tengo una hermana," she said to the empty kitchen, then wrinkled her nose. That was true, but it was only half true. She had a sister, Rosa, and a brother, Mateo. She chewed her pencil. The word for sister was hermana, and she was almost sure the word for brother was hermano. So how did you say both at once?

She tried the obvious thing. "Tengo una hermana y un hermano." It worked, she figured, but it sounded clunky, and Ms. Jean-Louis wanted them to sound natural. Anna stared at her notes. There had to be a shorter way, and she suspected the answer was hiding in the plural.

Grandpa shuffled in for coffee. "¿Qué haces, mija?"

"Practicando español," Anna said, and then, gathering her nerve, "Tengo dos hermanos."

Grandpa nodded like it was the most ordinary sentence in the world. "Sí, dos. Rosa y Mateo." He stirred his coffee and wandered back out, leaving Anna frozen at the table. Dos hermanos. Two. But Rosa wasn't a hermano, she was a hermana. Unless the plural word covered both. She flipped through her notes. Nothing. She texted Warren, whose abuela lived in Peru.

"Quick question," she typed. "If a girl has one brother and one sister, can she say tengo dos hermanos?"

His reply came fast. "That's what my cousin says all the time and it drove me crazy in September. I thought she was saying two brothers. I even told Reece she was lying about having a sister."

"So what changed your mind?"

"Reece asked her in class and she counted on her fingers. One hermano, one hermana, dos hermanos. I changed my mind on the spot."

Anna read it twice, then said the sentence out loud again, slower this time. "Tengo dos hermanos." It felt like a door had opened. The plural word could hold both of them at once. She wrote the sentence at the top of her page and underlined it.

For a while she'd been ready to resign herself to the long, clumsy version, the one with all the y's and un's, but now she had something cleaner. She drafted the rest on a napkin while the coffee maker hissed. "Tengo un perro. Mi perro es pequeño y reckless, corre por toda la casa." She laughed. Maybe reckless was pushing it, but Grandpa's chihuahua did knock over a lamp last month, so it was earned.

On Sunday she set up her phone on the cinnamon-scented table and pressed record. "Hola. Me llamo Anna. Tengo dos hermanos, una hermana y un hermano."

From the hallway, Grandpa's voice floated in. "¡Perfecto, mija!"

"¡Gracias!" Anna called back, and started the recording one more time, just to get it right.

Joshua slumped in the back row of the history classroom, staring at the poster assignment sheet like it had insulted him personally. Ms. Sato wanted each of them to analyze a wartime propaganda poster by Friday, and the only thing he knew about posters was that his little sister used them to cover crayon marks on her wall.

"Pick one from the box," Ms. Sato said, "then tell us what the poster wants you to believe and how it gets you to believe it."

Joshua dug through the box. He pulled out a poster of a smiling crowd with the words "Everyone Is Doing Their Part." Underneath it sat another one with a grim-looking soldier pointing straight at the viewer, captioned with words like "traitor" and "slacker." He held them both up. "These are weird," he said to Sullivan, who sat next to him flipping through posters of his own.

"Weird how?" Sullivan asked.

"Look, this one says everybody's doing something. That's not a reason, that's just... a crowd." Joshua frowned. "And this one calls people traitors for not buying something. Traitor is a big word. It's doing a lot of work."

Sehaj leaned over from the next row. "My poster has a movie star on it. Why is a movie star telling me to save scrap metal?"

"That's exactly my point!" Joshua said, louder than he meant to. Ms. Sato raised an eyebrow, and he lowered his voice. "There's a pattern here. The posters aren't arguing. They're just... pushing."

At lunch, Joshua scrolled through the library database for his research notes. He typed in "wartime posters persuasion" and got mostly stuff about advertising. He tried again and found a scanned page from a 1937 magazine. The Institute for Propaganda Analysis, it said, had been founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda. He read the sentence twice, then laughed out loud in the middle of the cafeteria, which earned him a look from the lunch monitor.

"What?" Sullivan said through a mouthful of fries.

"A whole institute," Joshua said. "People in 1937 were so tired of being tricked that they started an actual institute about it. It's like homework, but they invented it themselves."

Back in class on Friday, Joshua stood up with his two posters and Sehaj's movie star one, because Sehaj had agreed to trade for a poster with a tank on it. He taped them to the whiteboard. "Okay, so this one wants you to think you should join in because everyone else did." He tapped the crowd poster. "I'm calling that the Everybody's-Doing-It trick. This one uses loaded words, like traitor, to make you feel bad before you can even think." Then he pointed at the movie star. "And this one is just a famous person saying a thing, which famous people are not actually experts on."

He had one last thing. He held up his brittle, curling notebook page. "In 1937, some people got so annoyed by all this that they founded the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, right here in the United States, to teach the public how to recognize propaganda." He grinned. "They couldn't delete the posters, so they did the next best thing. They taught people to see through them."

"Like a revolution of not-believing-people," Sullivan offered.

"Sure," Joshua said. "A tiny revolution." He slapped the movie star poster back onto the board. "Next time a celebrity tells me to buy sneakers, I'm checking if they've ever made a sneaker."

Adrienne's kitchen had split into two armies, and Charlotte had not even taken off her coat yet.

"Tell her," Adrienne said, shoving a phone across the counter. "Tell her the dress is white and gold."

Charlotte looked down at the photo. A lacy dress, hanging on a hanger, lit strangely. She saw white and gold, obviously. Who wouldn't?

Charlotte looked again. Still white. Still gold. "You're messing with me."

"Why would I delegate the messing-with to my mother?" Adrienne said. "I do my own messing." She grabbed the phone and marched into the living room, where her older brother was sprawled on the couch. "Brinley's in the basement. We're doing a survey."

White and gold, white and gold, white and gold. Then she tilted the screen almost flat, and for one second, before her eyes snapped back, the dress went dark. Navy. Almost black.

"Adrienne," she said slowly. "Come here. Don't look at the dress. Look at me."

Adrienne rolled her eyes but did it. Charlotte tilted the phone up from her lap, fast, like showing a card trick. Adrienne blinked. Looked at the photo. Blinked again.

"That's not the same picture."

"It is."

"Charlotte, that dress is blue and black."

"Say that again."

"It's blue and black, and the one in February 2015 was blue and black too, and if you're about to tell me my mom was right, I'm going to lie down on this floor."

From the sink, without turning around, Adrienne's mother said, "The probability of that was always high, dear."

"Omar: why are you in the game store?"

Declan spun around. The mall was crowded, but nobody was looking at him. He typed back, "how do you know where I am?"

"Snap Map," Omar replied. "It shows your real-time location on a map. It's been on Snapchat since 2017."

Declan stared at his screen. A map, with his little face on it, parked right on top of the game store. He had never told anyone which store he was in. He felt like a bug under glass, the kind Omar's little sister would keep in a jar and poke with a venomous stick.

He decided to test it. He put the lens down, walked three stores down to the comic shop, and stood among the racks. A minute later, another buzz. "Omar: comic shop now? the Deadpool trade is behind the counter."

It worked. That was the strange part. It worked, and it kept working, and anyone on his friends list could watch him wander the mall like a dot on a screen. Declan thought about how many people were on that list, kids from school he barely knew, that boy from summer camp whose name he'd forgotten. His location, stored somewhere, shared somewhere, and he had never even noticed.

He found the settings and turned his location off, or at least he thought he did. Then he hurried to the register with a Deadpool trade, since Omar clearly wanted it, and texted, "meet me at the food court in ten. And no peeking at the map."

Back came one word: "deal." Declan ran for the escalator, the bag bumping his knee, and grinned the whole way down.

The box sat on the kitchen table between Beatrice and her mother, and Beatrice could hardly eat her toast. Her first phone, at last. She peeled off the plastic and turned the phone over in her hands while her mother talked about rules, minutes, and "this is not a toy." Beatrice was only half listening, because she was thinking about something Arianne had said at school: that people had carried phones in their pockets for only about fifty years. That seemed too short. Surely it was longer? She decided to test it with the phone itself.

"Can I text Arianne?" she asked, and her mother nodded. Beatrice typed, "How long have people had phones you can hold? Real answer please, not a guess." While she waited, she discovered that the family's old dictionary, which she had used to obstruct the wobbly table leg, made the phone slide unevenly when she set it down. She moved the book, and the phone sat flat. Small cause, small fix.

Arianne texted back: "My dad says the first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973. Beatrice checked the date against the calendar. So pocket phones really were only about fifty years old, and before that, phones sat on desks or hung on walls. She texted a follow-up question to make sure Arianne wasn't being gullible with some internet story, and Arianne sent a photo of a page from an actual book. The fact held.

Her mother slid a case across the table, thick foam padding like insulation around the phone. "You'll drop it," she said. "Everyone drops the first one." Beatrice snapped it on, then set her alarm for nine each night, phone charging in the kitchen, not her room, and wrote the rule on a sticky note by the door. When the screen lit up with a message from Melina asking about homework, Beatrice answered in one line, put the phone down, and finished her toast.

At school the next day, she told Arianne, "Martin Cooper, April 3, 1973, New York street, Motorola." Arianne grinned and said, "Look at you, phone owner and history expert both."

The notification buzzed while Marcus was pretending to do homework: 47 new messages in the Serrano Family Chat, which was mostly his aunts arguing about Thanksgiving and his grandmother saturating every thread with heart emojis until nobody wanted to argue anymore. He scrolled past all of it, because the app he really wanted to open was his old chat with Jayson. The last message was from five weeks ago. It said "lol" and nothing else, which was the vague kind of message that could mean anything, or nothing, which was exactly the problem.

They used to talk every day. Then Marcus made the soccer team and Jayson made the robotics team, and somehow every conversation since had gotten shorter, like a phone with a dying battery. Marcus didn't think they'd had a fight. That was the part that bugged him. How could a friendship break without anything breaking it?

He asked Cecilia at lunch, since she was the only person he knew who read actual studies for fun. She chewed her sandwich and nodded like he'd brought her a puzzle she'd already solved. "My sister told me about this," she said. "A 2015 study followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade, and the friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end." Marcus stared at his tray. Less alike. Different teams, different schedules, different everything lately. It wasn't a fight. It was drift, and drift had a pattern, which meant maybe a pattern could be reversed.

His technique, when he thought about it, was simple: don't message Jayson about robotics, which Marcus didn't understand, and don't apologize, which would be weird. Find the one thing they still had in common and lead with that. He thought hard. Not soccer. Not robots. Then it hit him, and he laughed out loud in the cafeteria like a weirdo, because of course: their old obsession with that terrible shark movie, the one they'd watched nine times and ranked the rubber sharks from worst to slightly less worst.

That night he opened the family chat first, where his plan was already under construction. He'd posted a poll: "SHARK MOVIE SEQUEL: yes or yes." His aunt had voted. His grandmother had voted twice somehow. His mom had replied "Marcus, homework." Then, before he could lose his nerve, he screenshotted the poll and sent it to Jayson with one line: "The family demands a viewing. Saturday. My basement. Bring your own skepticism about shark physics."

The typing bubble appeared, vanished, appeared again. Marcus held his breath so long his ears popped. Then: "Only if we do the commentary track where we rank every shark again. Steel Shark is still last and I will die on this hill." Marcus grinned so wide it hurt, and in the family chat, his grandmother had already sent three more hearts.
